items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: Benny did the score for a movie, and Mel Torme was in the movie. So anyway we were recording the soundtrack, a period of about three days I guess.

ctx.x: I want to ask you about young keyboard artists coming up today, who do you like? Who do you think carries on the tradition and has a good feel, a good grasp on the music?

There are a lot of young artists today. There’s a lot of them. Benny Green for one, a young piano player. And there’s another one, what’s this kid’s name, a heavy set guy, I’ll think of his name in a minute. Steven Scott is another one that I like. And then there are a lot of them who don’t have big names yet. There was one I had as a student at the New School and he’s recording on Verve now. He’s also playing organ. That’s Larry Goldings. He’s another one. There are so many of them. I don’t know I listen to…
Do you have a favorite record of your own?

items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: it was a tribute to Benny Carter cruise, and the three of us played and we accompanied Benny and did nights by ourselves.

ctx.x: No. Not really. I didn’t know what to call it, and then “Harlem Lullaby” stuck. But believe it or not I just recorded it again and I did it on this live session. And the producer liked it so well that I just did a record for them a few months ago. It should be out either this month or next month. And he asked me would I do it again for the session, I mean in the studio, and I did it. And I would have to send you that one because you know after you’ve done a tune a lot, then sometimes it either gets better or…

session. For one thing, recording for Enja, this particular producer I had, Horst Weber out of Munich, he insists on any, even in the studio, it’s almost like doing a live date because he will only use first takes. And just by coincidence he has the same idea about recording, which is, when you’ve got to do two or three takes, and I’ve always had this idea, if I have to repeat a thing, it goes downhill. Usually the first take, you’ve got the feeling that you want. You may miss a few notes. Horst doesn’t care. He…
